one_liner: C++17 sparse linear algebra library with portable CUDA/HIP/SYCL/OpenMP kernels; beat AmgX AMG and MAGMA batched solves in DOE apps.
what_it_does: Ginkgo is a sparse linear-algebra framework built around a LinOp abstraction: matrices (CSR, COO, ELL, hybrid, dense and more), Krylov solvers (CG, BiCGStab, GMRES and others), preconditioners (block-Jacobi, ILU/IC, AMG), sparse direct LU/Cholesky, and batched solvers all compose as linear operators. An Executor object (Reference, OMP, CUDA, HIP, DPC++) picks where kernels run, and the same user code runs on NVIDIA, AMD and Intel GPUs or CPUs. It is not a drop-in replacement for SuiteSparse, Eigen or PETSc; you build operators through Ginkgo's own factory API (or the separate pyGinkgo Python bindings).
how_it_is_fast: Each backend gets hand-written kernels for its hardware (CUDA, HIP, SYCL), so nothing goes through a generic translation layer. The speedups in the measured cases come from mixed-precision AMG (coarse levels in lower precision, fine level in full precision, parallel graph-matching coarsening), batched iterative solvers that solve many small independent sparse systems inside one GPU kernel, and GPU-resident sparse direct factorization and triangular solves. Half and bfloat16 value types, plus adaptive-precision block-Jacobi, cut memory traffic in these memory-bound kernels.
when_to_use: Iterative solves of large sparse systems on NVIDIA, AMD or Intel GPUs where you want one codebase across vendors
Many small independent sparse systems per step (chemistry or combustion kinetics, per-cell plasma solves) through the batched BiCGStab/GMRES solvers
Replacing NVIDIA AmgX with a vendor-neutral AMG preconditioner, especially in mixed precision
Moving a CPU sparse direct solve (MA57- or LAPACK-banded-style) onto GPUs to remove host-device round trips
Distributed solves via the MPI module (GPU-aware MPI recommended)
when_not_to_use: Small or one-off CPU-only sparse solves: Eigen/SuiteSparse are simpler, and no CPU-vs-SuiteSparse benchmark is cited
Sparse direct factorization of hard 3D problems: the IJHPCA paper says the direct solvers lack supernodal techniques, so CHOLMOD/MUMPS-class solvers are likely stronger
AMG needing aggressive or alternative coarsening: only parallel graph-matching coarsening is supported per the paper
Strong scaling on many nodes: the paper names communication as the bottleneck
Builds with limited compile time or memory: full GPU builds are heavy (INSTALL.md warns of >20 min and high memory for the Jacobi kernels with full optimizations)

integration.form: shared lib (static optional via BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=OFF); CMake find_package(Ginkgo), target Ginkgo::ginkgo
integration.dependencies: none for the core/reference build; optional CUDA 11+, ROCm 6.2+ (hipBLAS, hipSPARSE, rocRAND, rocThrust), oneAPI 2024.1+ (oneMKL, oneDPL), OpenMP, MPI 3.1+, METIS, PAPI
integration.min_toolchain: C++17; CMake 3.16+; GCC 7+, Clang 5+, Intel 2019+, MSVC 2019+, NVHPC 22.7+
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows; x86-64/aarch64 CPUs (OpenMP); NVIDIA (CUDA), AMD (HIP), Intel (SYCL) GPUs

gotchas: Half precision needs CUDA compute capability 5.3+ and bfloat16 needs 8.0+ unless built with CUDA 12.2+
GINKGO_JACOBI_FULL_OPTIMIZATIONS gives the best adaptive block-Jacobi but greatly increases compile time and memory
Windows builds can hit 'export ordinal too large' (needs -O1) and cc1plus out-of-memory errors
The headline numbers come from application integrations (MFEM, PeleLM, XGC, ExaSGD), not from a standalone kernel shootout
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Choose Ginkgo over AMGCL when you need full solver stacks on AMD or Intel GPUs, batched small-system solvers, or mixed-precision AMG. Choose it over CSR5, merge-spmv or ISpMV when you need complete solvers and preconditioners rather than one SpMV kernel, and over BaSpaCho or Sympiler when an iterative or batched method fits better than a supernodal Cholesky.
verified_claims_summary: The IJHPCA 2024 ECP paper reports: Ginkgo AMG with 20-40% faster per-iteration preconditioner application than NVIDIA AmgX on a V100 (MFEM), and mixed-precision AMG 1.5x faster on one L-shape case; batched BiCGStab about 2x over MAGMA's batched dense direct solve in PeleLM (MI250X, Frontier); about 90% less linear-solver time than LAPACK dgbsv in XGC (Perlmutter A100, Crusher MI250X); and 1.8-2.4x end-to-end over a CPU MA57 baseline on MI250X for ACOPF (1.05-1.3x on V100). That last result compares GPU against CPU. Compiler flags are not stated.
status_note: Actively developed (612 stars, commits through 2026-09) under BSD-3-Clause with an OpenSSF best-practices badge and CI on GitLab, so it is safe to adopt as a dependency, but it is too large to vendor as source.
